## Part A: Fill-in README / deck template

Use this as your repo README and as the outline of a 6-slide deck. Fill every field; if you cannot, that is the gap to close before the interview. Unmeasured items must be labelled **estimate** or **not measured**.

```markdown
# <Project name>: one-line description

## 1. Problem and users
- User: <who, concretely>
- Workflow before: <what they did, time/cost/error>
- Success criterion (set before building): <metric and threshold>

## 2. Architecture
- Diagram: <image or mermaid, request path numbered 1..n>
- Components: <name: one-sentence job> (max 6)
- Data flow: <ingest -> store -> retrieve -> generate -> validate>
- External dependencies: <providers, APIs, versions>

## 3. My contribution
- I designed: ...
- I implemented: ...
- I tested / evaluated: ...
- I deployed / operated: ...
- Not mine (team / library): ...

## 4. Key decisions
| Decision | Options | Chosen | Why (evidence) | Cost of the choice |
|---|---|---|---|---|

## 5. Evaluation
- Dataset: <n questions, source, labelling method, who labelled>
- Baseline: <what, same dataset>
- Results: <metric: value, 95% interval, n>
- Error categories: <table with counts>
- Limits: <what this does not show>

## 6. Reliability and security
- Timeouts / retries / rate limits: ...
- Permissions: ...
- Prompt injection: <threat, control, residual risk>
- Secrets: ...
- Failure behaviour: <what the user sees>

## 7. Performance and cost
- Latency: <measured: method, n, p50/p95>  OR  <estimate: assumptions>
- Cost: <measured OR estimate with token counts and price variables>

## 8. Failure story
- Symptom -> Investigation -> Root cause -> Fix -> Prevention

## 9. Next improvements
- <improvement>: justified if <evidence>
```

Repo skeleton that supports the template:

## Part B: Fully worked fictional example

**This is an illustrative example project. The project, its numbers and its bug are invented to show the shape of a good answer. Do not reuse the numbers; replace them with your own measurements.**

**Project: "DocsAsk", a Q&A assistant over a product's public documentation.** Built solo as a portfolio project, deployed as a small web app with about 20 test users from a developer community.

### 1. Problem and users

Users are developers integrating a fictional payments SDK. Before: they searched a 400-page docs site and the issue tracker, which took several minutes and often ended in a forum post. Success criterion, set before building: at least 80 percent of answerable questions answered correctly with a citation that supports the claim, and the system says "I do not know" for questions the docs do not cover.

### 2. Architecture

Request path: (1) browser sends question to a FastAPI service; (2) the service rewrites the question lightly and runs hybrid retrieval (keyword plus vector) in Postgres with pgvector; (3) top 30 candidates are reranked with a cross-encoder to the top 5; (4) the prompt is built with the 5 chunks, each tagged with an id; (5) the model is called with a timeout and returns JSON with `answer` and `citations` (chunk ids); (6) a validator checks that cited ids exist in the retrieved set and that the answer is not empty when evidence exists; (7) the response streams back. Ingestion is a script that crawls the docs, splits by heading, stores chunks with `content_hash`, and re-embeds only changed chunks. External dependencies: one model provider API and one embedding API.

### 3. My contribution

I designed the chunking and retrieval pipeline, implemented the service, the ingestion script and the evaluation harness, wrote the tests, and deployed with Docker Compose on one VM. I used a hosted embedding model and a hosted LLM; I did not train anything. The docs content is public and not mine.

### 4. Key decisions

| Decision | Options | Chosen | Why | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAG vs fine-tuning | Fine-tune on docs; RAG | RAG | Docs change weekly; need citations; fine-tuning does not give sources | Retrieval quality becomes the bottleneck |
| Vector store | Dedicated vector DB; pgvector | pgvector | Corpus is about 6,000 chunks; I already needed Postgres; simpler to operate | Would revisit at millions of vectors |
| Retrieval | Vector only; keyword only; hybrid | Hybrid | In my test set, error codes and function names were missed by vector-only search (see error table) | Two indexes to maintain |
| Reranker | None; cross-encoder | Cross-encoder over top 30 | Improved correctness in the experiment below | About 200 ms extra (measured on my machine) |
| Framework | Orchestration framework; plain code | Plain Python plus a small client library | The pipeline is a straight line; fewer moving parts to debug | I wrote the retry code myself |
| Chunking | Fixed 500 tokens; by heading | By heading with a size cap | Fixed chunks cut code samples in half | Longer chunks for big sections |

### 5. Evaluation

- **Dataset:** 60 questions: 52 answerable and 8 deliberately unanswerable. I wrote 40 from the docs and 20 from real questions in the community forum. I labelled gold passages myself, which is a bias; a second labeller checked 15 of them and agreed on 13.
- **Baseline:** keyword-only search (BM25) with the same generator and prompt.
- **Results (n = 60, correct answer or correct abstention):**

| System | Correct | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|
| Keyword-only baseline | 41/60 = 68% | 56% to 79% |
| Hybrid + rerank (final) | 48/60 = 80% | 68% to 88% |

The intervals overlap. A paired comparison is more informative: 11 questions flipped from wrong to right and 4 from right to wrong, so net +7. That is suggestive, not proof, at this sample size; I would add 100 more questions before claiming a gain.

- **Error categories for the final system (12 errors):** retrieval miss 5, wrong chunk ranked above right one 3, hallucinated detail despite correct chunk 2, failed to abstain 1, formatting 1.
- **Limits:** questions come from one product; I wrote most of them; no multilingual coverage; no multi-turn conversations tested.

### 6. Reliability and security

Timeouts: 20 seconds on the model call, 5 seconds on retrieval. Retries: up to 2 with backoff and jitter on 429 and 5xx only; no retry after tokens have started streaming. Rate limit: 20 requests per hour per IP at the proxy. Prompt injection: the documents are public but user-editable pages (community wiki, if included) could carry instructions, so retrieved text is delimited and labelled as data, the model has no tools, and the answer is validated; the worst case is a wrong answer, not an action. A test feeds a chunk containing "ignore previous instructions" and checks the answer still cites correctly (it passed; I treat this as one data point, not a guarantee). Secrets: provider keys in environment variables injected at deploy, not in the repo; request logs store question length and ids, not content. Failure behaviour: if the model is down, the UI shows the top 3 retrieved passages with a notice.

### 7. Performance and cost

Measured: 30 requests from my laptop to the deployed service, p50 3.1 s and p95 5.8 s to the full response, about 1.4 s to first streamed token. Cost: **not measured in production**. Estimate from token counts logged during the evaluation run (average about 2,600 input and 280 output tokens) and placeholder prices of 2 and 8 USD per million tokens: roughly 0.0075 USD per question. At 1,000 questions a month that would be about 7.50 USD; I would verify against actual billing.

### 8. Failure story

**Symptom:** after I re-ingested the docs, some answers cited a deprecated endpoint that had been removed from the site. **Investigation:** I logged retrieved chunk ids for those questions and found chunks with the old text still in the index. **Root cause:** the ingestion script upserted changed pages but never deleted chunks for pages that had disappeared, so removed content stayed searchable. **Fix:** ingestion now computes the set of live document ids, soft-deletes chunks for missing ones immediately, then hard-deletes them. **Prevention:** a test that ingests a corpus, removes a page, re-ingests, and asserts the page's chunks are unretrievable; plus a nightly check that compares index document ids against the site's sitemap.

### 9. Next improvements

First, enlarge the eval set to 200 questions with a second labeller, because the current sample cannot distinguish a 5 point change. Second, if the error table still shows retrieval misses above about 25 percent of errors, try query rewriting and test it against the paired metric. I would not add agents or multi-hop reasoning without evidence that users ask such questions.

## Part C: The code for honest reporting

`eval_report.py` computes recall, correctness and citation accuracy **with Wilson 95 percent intervals** and counts errors by category, so every number you quote carries its denominator and uncertainty. `test_eval_report.py` pins the interval arithmetic (for example 48 of 60 gives about 68 to 88 percent), the zero-sample case and the answerable-only denominators. Run with `pip install pytest` then `pytest -q` (3 tests). In your own project, feed it real per-question results and paste the output into the README's Evaluation section.

## Exercises

1. Fill in the template for your own project in full. Mark each unmeasured item.
2. Time yourself delivering the five-minute demo. Cut anything that does not fit.
3. Write your failure story in the five-part form, one sentence per part, then expand to 60 seconds spoken.
4. Run your eval results through `report()` and rewrite your claims with intervals.
5. Ask a friend to ask the 25 questions below; record yourself; note every "um, I think".

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. The five-minute demo was twelve minutes of scrolling a notebook. Contribution was 'we built'. The README listed libraries. A hard follow-up ('what would you delete?') got 'nothing, it is all needed'. Numbers were from a single cherry-picked query. The candidate could not open the eval file. Red flags (framework-first, no failure) were all present and unnoticed.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'What is the riskiest part of this system, and what did you measure?' Outline: name the stage (retrieval, tools, cost), the metric, the number, and the change you shipped. Follow-up: 'What did someone else do?' Draw a clean line. If you cannot, say so.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut the library tour and any number you did not measure. Keep a nine-section story, a timed five-minute demo, and one failure with a metric.

"""Turn per-question eval results into an honest report: rates WITH uncertainty, by error category."""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass


def wilson_interval(successes: int, n: int, z: float = 1.96) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """95% Wilson score interval for a proportion. Wide interval = small sample; say so."""
    if n == 0:
        return (0.0, 1.0)
    p = successes / n
    denom = 1 + z * z / n
    centre = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / denom
    half = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / denom
    return (max(0.0, centre - half), min(1.0, centre + half))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Result:
    qid: str
    answerable: bool
    gold_in_top_k: bool      # was the gold passage retrieved?
    correct: bool            # human-judged answer correctness (or abstained correctly)
    cited_ok: bool           # every citation exists and supports the claim
    error: str | None = None  # category when not correct: retrieval_miss, wrong_chunk, hallucination, ...


def report(results: list[Result]) -> dict:
    answerable = [r for r in results if r.answerable]
    n_all = len(results)
    out = {
        "n": n_all,
        "n_answerable": len(answerable),
        "recall_at_k": rate(sum(r.gold_in_top_k for r in answerable), len(answerable)),
        "correct": rate(sum(r.correct for r in results), n_all),
        "citation_accuracy": rate(sum(r.cited_ok for r in answerable), len(answerable)),
        "errors": dict(Counter(r.error for r in results if r.error)),
    }
    return out


def rate(successes: int, n: int) -> dict:
    lo, hi = wilson_interval(successes, n)
    return {"value": round(successes / n, 3) if n else None, "ci95": (round(lo, 3), round(hi, 3)), "n": n}

import math

from eval_report import Result, report, wilson_interval


def test_wilson_interval_is_wide_for_small_samples():
    lo, hi = wilson_interval(8, 10)
    assert math.isclose(lo, 0.490, abs_tol=0.005) and math.isclose(hi, 0.943, abs_tol=0.005)
    lo60, hi60 = wilson_interval(48, 60)
    assert hi60 - lo60 < hi - lo          # more data, narrower interval
    assert 0.67 < lo60 < 0.69 and 0.88 < hi60 < 0.90


def test_zero_samples_gives_the_uninformative_interval():
    assert wilson_interval(0, 0) == (0.0, 1.0)


def test_report_counts_errors_and_separates_answerable_questions():
    rs = [
        Result("q1", True, True, True, True),
        Result("q2", True, False, False, False, "retrieval_miss"),
        Result("q3", True, True, False, False, "hallucination"),
        Result("q4", False, False, True, True),   # unanswerable, correctly abstained
    ]
    r = report(rs)
    assert r["n"] == 4 and r["n_answerable"] == 3
    assert r["recall_at_k"]["value"] == round(2 / 3, 3)
    assert r["errors"] == {"retrieval_miss": 1, "hallucination": 1}

parts.body:
## How to use this part

Interviewers drill into whatever you say. For each section below there are hard follow-ups with a way to answer. The pattern for any question you cannot answer from measurement is:

1. **State what you did know or measure.**
2. **Say plainly what you did not measure.**
3. **Explain how you would find out** (a specific experiment, metric, sample size).
4. **Give your current best belief and label it a belief.**

Example: "I did not measure that. What I know is that on my 60-question set the retrieval miss rate was 5 of 60. To know whether a reranker helps beyond that, I would run a paired comparison on a larger set. My expectation is yes, but I would treat that as a hypothesis."

## Problem and users

1. **Who actually used this, and how do you know?** Answer with real counts and sources ("about 20 people from the forum; I have 140 logged questions") or say it is a portfolio project with no real users and describe who the target user would be and how you simulated their questions.
2. **Why was this a problem worth solving with an LLM?** Compare with keyword search or a better docs layout; say what the LLM adds (natural-language questions, synthesis across pages) and what it costs.
3. **How did you define success, and when?** Name the criterion and that it was set before building; if it was not, say so and explain what you would set now.
4. **What would make you say this project failed?** A threshold on the metric, a user complaint pattern, or cost per question; have one.

## Architecture

5. **Walk me through one request end to end.** Use the numbered request path; mention timeouts and where validation happens.
6. **Why this component split? What would you remove?** Name one piece you would drop for v1 and why; shows judgement.
7. **Where does state live, and what happens on restart?** Be exact: database tables, in-memory caches that are lost, idempotency.
8. **What are your external dependencies and what if one is down?** Provider outage behaviour, fallback, degraded mode.
9. **How does data get in, and how do updates and deletions propagate?** Describe change detection, deletion handling and the bug it prevented (a good place for the failure story).

## Your contribution

10. **What did you personally write versus use from a library?** Be precise; name the library functions you rely on; be ready to describe what they do underneath.
11. **Show me the hardest function you wrote.** Pick one in advance, know its edge cases and tests.
12. **If this was a team project, what did the others do?** Describe their parts accurately; do not claim them.

## Key decisions

13. **Why RAG and not fine-tuning?** Freshness, citations and cost of updating; fine-tuning teaches style and format more than facts. Say you did not try fine-tuning if you did not.
14. **Why that chunk size?** Give your reason and, if you tested it, the result; if not, "I chose heading-based chunks to keep code samples intact; I did not run a chunk-size sweep. I would sweep 3 sizes and compare recall at k."
15. **Why that model? Did you compare?** If you compared, give the set and result; if not, say it was a default chosen for cost and availability, and describe the comparison you would run (same eval set, same prompt, cost and latency recorded).
16. **Why a framework (or why not)?** Reasons grounded in the problem: "straight-line pipeline, so plain code was easier to debug". If you used one, explain what it did that you would otherwise write.
17. **Why pgvector and not a dedicated vector DB?** Corpus size, operational simplicity, filtering with SQL; and the scale at which you would revisit.
18. **What simpler alternative did you reject, and why?** Have one genuine answer: keyword search was the baseline you beat by a measured margin.

## Evaluation

19. **How big is your test set and where did the questions come from?** Give n and sources and the bias (you wrote them). Mention the second labeller if any.
20. **How do you know the improvement is real and not noise?** Intervals, paired comparison, more data; admit when the sample is too small.
21. **How do you measure groundedness or hallucination?** Citation validation in code (ids exist) plus human check of whether the cited chunk supports the claim on a sample; admit limits of any automated judge.
22. **Did you use an LLM as a judge? How did you validate it?** If yes, compare with human labels on a sample and report agreement; if no, say so.
23. **What does your test set not cover?** Multi-turn, other languages, adversarial inputs, very long questions; be specific.
24. **What was your biggest error category and what did you do about it?** Use the error table with counts.

## Reliability and security

25. **What happens if the retrieved text contains instructions?** Delimiting, no tools, output validation, the test you ran, and the honest limit.
26. **How do you stop one user from running up your bill?** Rate limits at the proxy, token caps per request, daily budget alert; if not implemented, say what you would add.
27. **How do you handle provider timeouts and 429s?** Timeouts per stage, bounded retries with backoff and jitter, no retry after streaming started.
28. **Where are your secrets and what do your logs contain?** Environment or secret manager; logs hold ids and lengths, not content.
29. **Could a user see another user's data?** Describe the isolation model; if single-tenant and public data, say so and explain what would change for private data.

## Performance and cost

30. **What is your p95 latency?** Quote it only with method and n; otherwise "I measured 30 requests on my laptop; I do not have production numbers".
31. **What does a query cost?** Show the token arithmetic with price variables and label it an estimate unless billing confirms it.
32. **Where would you cut cost or latency first?** The biggest lever from your numbers: context size, caching, smaller model for easy cases, streaming for perceived latency.

## Failure story and next steps

33. **Tell me about a bug that taught you something.** Five-part story; end with the prevention (a test, a monitor).
34. **What would you do with another month?** The highest-value item and the evidence that would justify it.
35. **What would you do differently if you started over?** Build the eval set first; log retrieved ids from day one; pick one thing you really would change.

## Honest-answer phrases that work

- "I did not measure that. Here is what I measured, and here is how I would measure the rest."
- "That was a judgement call; I did not test the alternative. My reason was X, and I would test it with Y."
- "That part was my teammate's. My understanding of it is ..., but I would defer to them on details."
- "My sample is 60 questions, so I treat the difference as suggestive."
- "I do not know. My first step would be ..."

## Phrases and habits to avoid

- "It works really well" (say how you know).
- "Production-ready" (say what scale, uptime, users).
- "State of the art", "cutting edge", "agentic" without a mechanism.
- Listing every library you touched.
- Inventing a number when probed. If you do not have it, say so.

## 60-90 second spoken pitch (template)

"I built X for Y, who had the problem that Z, which took them about N before. I set a success criterion of C. The system works like this: [numbered flow, one sentence each]. My part was [specific list]. The key decisions were [two, with reasons and the simpler alternative I rejected]. I evaluated it on N questions from [source] against a baseline of B: [result with interval]. The biggest error category was E at K cases. For production I handled [timeouts, retries, permissions, injection] and I measured latency at [number, method] but I only estimated cost at [number, assumptions]. A bug that taught me something: [one-line symptom to prevention]. Next I would [improvement] if [evidence]."

Rehearse it until you can say it in 75 seconds without notes, then rehearse answering interruptions at every sentence.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Interview tab: a spoken-answer failure, the actual next question, and the essay you would not say out loud. The five-minute demo was twelve minutes of scrolling a notebook. Contribution was 'we built'. The README listed libraries. A hard follow-up ('what would you delete?') got 'nothing, it is all needed'. Numbers were from a single cherry-picked query. The candidate could not open the eval file. Red flags (framework-first, no failure) were all present and unnoticed.

## Interview follow-up

You already gave a 90-second answer; this is the probe. Interviewer: 'What is the riskiest part of this system, and what did you measure?' Outline: name the stage (retrieval, tools, cost), the metric, the number, and the change you shipped. Follow-up: 'What did someone else do?' Draw a clean line. If you cannot, say so.

## What you would cut

Say less: keep define, mechanism, decision, trade-off, evidence. Cut the library tour and any number you did not measure. Keep a nine-section story, a timed five-minute demo, and one failure with a metric.

# Drills

Stand up. Five minutes on the clock. No slides. Then take one hard follow-up without looking at notes.

## Prompt 1 — closed-book

"Walk me through a GenAI project you built, as if I will probe it for twenty minutes."

**Model outline:**
1. **Problem and user.** Who felt the pain, how they do it now.
2. **Your part.** One sentence that would still be true if a teammate were in the room.
3. **Design.** Retrieve / generate / tools; where the risk is.
4. **Eval.** The set, the metric, the number, the gate.
5. **Failure.** What broke, how you saw it, what you changed.
6. **Trade-off.** Something you did not build, and why.
7. **Demo beat.** One query, one citation or tool trace, one miss you handle.
8. **Honest gap.** What is prototype versus production.

**Grade:** fail if you say "we built" with no "I", or if every number is unsourced.

## Prompt 2 — closed-book

"What would you delete from this project tomorrow, and how would you know it was safe?"

**Model outline:**
1. **Candidate cut.** A stage (reranker, extra tool, long history) that did not move the eval.
2. **Metric.** Which score must stay flat (citation support, task success, p95, cost per query).
3. **Method.** A/B or a replay of the golden set on a branch without that stage.
4. **Rollback.** Feature flag or previous graph revision.
5. **Would not cut.** Permission filters, refuse-when-unsupported, or the audit log.
6. **Evidence.** A real or hypothetical number; if hypothetical, say so.

Write the two answers as bullets in your README. If you cannot fill the numbers, that is the project's next work, not a wording problem.

Leadership title held during the project

Linked evidence from your resume

It makes the story too short
It signals that you disliked your teammates

> **Outcome:** Build 6 to 8 truthful STAR-L stories covering eight themes, rehearse 90-second and 3-minute versions, and handle follow-ups.
> **Prerequisites:** None.
> **Estimated time:** 40 min reading, then the hands-on task. Apply it once in your next weekly review or mock, using the lesson's worked example or template.

## Why a story bank

Behavioural rounds are not a personality test; they are structured evidence collection. The interviewer asks "tell me about a time when..." and scores your answer against a rubric: did you take **ownership**, was your **judgement** sound, can you **communicate**, do you **learn**. Strong technical candidates lose offers here because they improvise, ramble, say "we" for everything, or tell a story with no result. The fix is preparation: a **bank of 6 to 8 true stories**, each rehearsed in a 90-second and a 3-minute version, that together cover the common themes. In the interview you do not memorise answers; you recognise the question's theme and pull the matching story.

The one rule that overrides everything: **truth**. Use real work. Do not invent metrics, leadership scope or outcomes. Interviewers follow up on specifics ("what was your exact role? who disagreed? what happened after?"), and an invented story collapses under the second question. A modest true story told precisely beats a heroic one told vaguely.

## The STAR-L structure

STAR is Situation, Task, Action, Result. **STAR-L adds Learning**, which matters most for experienced candidates because it shows you improve the system and yourself, not only fix the incident.

| Letter | Answer | Typical share of time | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S**ituation | Context in two sentences: team, system, stakes | 15% | Backstory that eats the time |
| **T**ask | What *you* were responsible for and why it was hard | 10% | Confusing the team's goal with your task |
| **A**ction | What *you personally did*, step by step, with the reasoning behind decisions | 45% | "We", and listing activity without decisions |
| **R**esult | What changed, with evidence; honest if partial | 20% | No result, or an unsourced number |
| **L**earning | What you changed afterwards (habit, process, design) | 10% | Generic lessons ("communication is key") |

### The five-bullet card for each story

Write each story as five bullets, nothing more, so you can retell it without a script:

1. **Context:** system, team size, what was at stake.
2. **Responsibility:** your role and the specific problem you owned.
3. **Actions you personally took:** 3 to 5 steps, with a decision and a reason in each.
4. **Result and evidence:** what changed; the measurement or artifact that shows it; if partial or negative, say so.
5. **Lesson:** a concrete thing you now do differently, ideally one you can point to later in your career.

### Timing

At a comfortable speaking pace of about 130 to 150 words per minute, a **90-second version is roughly 200 words** and a **3-minute version roughly 350 to 450 words**. Practise out loud with a timer; reading silently misleads you. Version 1 (90 s) is for "tell me about a time..." as a first answer. Version 2 (3 min) is for when the interviewer says "tell me more" or when you are asked to go deep. In both, put the **result early** if the story is long ("we cut recovery time from hours to minutes; here is how").

## The eight themes and what the interviewer listens for

| Theme | Prompt example | Strong signal |
|---|---|---|
| **Ownership** | A feature or service you drove from ambiguity to delivery | You defined the problem, made decisions with incomplete information, and followed through to adoption |
| **Debugging** | A production issue you diagnosed systematically | Hypotheses, evidence, narrowing, root cause rather than a lucky fix, and prevention |
| **Conflict** | Disagreement with a teammate or stakeholder | You understood their goal, used data or a prototype, aligned or disagreed and committed, kept the relationship |
| **Failure** | A decision or implementation that did not work | You own the part that was yours, no blaming, concrete change afterwards |
| **Prioritization** | Competing deadlines or tech debt | A criteria-based decision, communicated trade-offs, said no or deferred explicitly |
| **Learning** | New technology learned and applied | A learning method, a small application, evidence you actually used it |
| **Communication** | Translated technical risk for a non-technical stakeholder | You adapted language, quantified risk, and obtained a decision |
| **Quality** | Tests, monitoring or process changes that prevented repeat failure | You moved from reacting to preventing, with something that still exists |

For AI engineering roles, add three flavoured prompts that interviewers increasingly ask: **a time an LLM feature misbehaved**, **a time you pushed back on hype**, and **a time you chose the simpler solution**. Examples of each are in the Interview section. They map onto themes: misbehaved is debugging plus quality; pushed back on hype is communication plus conflict; simpler solution is prioritization plus ownership.

## Building the bank: a process

1. **Brain-dump 15 to 20 episodes** from the last 3 to 4 years: incidents, launches, disagreements, mistakes, migrations, things you learned, times you said no.
2. **Score each** on: Was my role clear and personal? Is there a result or evidence? Can I be honest about it? Is it recent enough? Does it have an interesting decision?
3. **Pick 6 to 8** and map them to the eight themes so every theme has a primary story and, ideally, a backup (see the matrix in the Worked example). One story can serve two or three themes with different emphasis; a story that fits only one theme is fine, but avoid needing the same story for every question.
4. **Write the five-bullet card**, then the 90-second version, then the 3-minute version.
5. **Check truth and numbers**: every number has a source (a dashboard, ticket, commit, a colleague who can confirm). If you cannot source a number, say "roughly" or drop it. If the real result was modest or mixed, keep it that way.
6. **Rehearse aloud with a timer**, ideally with a friend who asks the follow-ups from the bank in the Interview section. Record yourself once; listen for "we", filler, and missing results.
7. **Refresh monthly**, and add stories from new work, especially AI work, as you build it.

## What "good" sounds like

- **"I" for what you did, "we" for what the team did, and be explicit about the boundary.**
- A **decision with a reason**: "I chose X over Y because Z".
- A **number or artifact** in the result, or an honest "I did not measure it; here is how I know it helped".
- **Specific learning**: "Now every release has a canary and an owner" rather than "I learned to communicate".
- **No villains.** Describe the other person's goals fairly. Interviewers infer how you would talk about them.

## Failure modes

Mistakes are covered fully in the Interview section: we versus I, no result, blame, memorised monologues, and stories that are too old or too trivial. The structural failure is having 2 stories stretched across all prompts; the tactical failure is a story that sounds good but that you cannot defend under questions.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. The stories were generic ('we had a tight deadline'). Action was a team we. Result had no number. Learning was 'communication is important'. Two stories contradicted the resume's dates. A conflict story blamed the other person. There were four stories, all from the same project, so a probe into a different company left them inventing.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer: 'Tell me about a time you were wrong.' Outline: situation with a real constraint, the task you owned, the action you took (including the mistake), the result with a number or a clear outcome, and the learning you applied later. Follow-up: 'What would you do in the first week here?' Tie the learning to their environment, not a slogan.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut borrowed stories and a sixth clone of the same incident. Keep six to eight true STAR-L cards that cover ownership, conflict, failure, and prioritisation, each with a result you can defend.

## The template

Copy this for each story. Fill in your real facts; leave a field blank rather than invent.

```text
STORY TITLE:
THEMES (primary first):
1 CONTEXT:         system, team, stakes (2 sentences)
2 RESPONSIBILITY:  my role, the problem I owned
3 ACTIONS I TOOK:  step + decision + reason (3 to 5 steps, "I")
4 RESULT/EVIDENCE: what changed; source of any number; honest limits
5 LESSON:          what I now do differently
FOLLOW-UP PREP:    who disagreed, what I would redo, what I did not know, who can confirm
90-SECOND VERSION: about 200 words, result stated clearly
3-MINUTE VERSION:  about 350 to 450 words, adds the reasoning behind two decisions
```

The `story_bank.py` file lints cards in this shape: all five fields present, "we" not outnumbering "I" in the actions, numbers having a source, and which themes are uncovered or covered by only one story. Run `python story_bank.py` to see it pass its own tests, then feed it your cards.

## Illustrative story A (fictional): debugging a production issue

**This is a fictional example to show structure. Do not reuse its details; replace them with your own true story.**

**Five-bullet card**
1. **Context:** A checkout API for a mid-size shop, four engineers, I was on call. After a Tuesday release, customers saw slow payment pages.
2. **Responsibility:** I was the on-call engineer and the owner of the order service.
3. **Actions:** I checked the dashboard and saw p95 had doubled only on one endpoint (decision: narrow before guessing). I compared traces before and after the release and saw time moving into a database call (decision: test the release diff, not infrastructure). I found a new query that ran once per order item, an N+1 pattern. I shipped a fix batching the query and added an index, after reproducing the slowdown locally with a script.
4. **Result:** p95 returned to its earlier level the same afternoon, verified on the dashboard. I added a regression test that fails if the query count per request exceeds a limit. (Fictional example, no real measurements.)
5. **Lesson:** Compare against the last known good version before forming theories, and put query-count assertions around hot paths.

**90-second version (about 200 words)**

"After a release on a Tuesday, our checkout pages got slow. I was on call and owned the order service, so I took it. My first decision was to narrow before guessing: on the dashboard, p95 had doubled on one endpoint only, the order summary. That ruled out infrastructure. Second, I compared traces from before and after the release and saw the extra time was in a single database call. Third, I read the release diff and found a new query that ran once for every item in an order, a classic N plus one pattern, invisible in testing because test orders had one item.

I reproduced it locally with a script that created a ten-item order, then batched the query and added an index. After deploying, p95 returned to normal the same afternoon, which I confirmed on the dashboard. To keep it from coming back I added a test that fails if a request issues more than a set number of queries.

The lesson I took is to compare against the last known good version before forming theories, and to protect hot paths with a cheap automated check."

**3-minute version (about 360 words)**

"This was a checkout API for a mid-size online shop; four backend engineers, and that week I was on call. On Tuesday afternoon, support reported slow payment pages. The stakes were direct: slow checkout means abandoned carts. I owned the order service, so I took the incident.

I started by narrowing the problem rather than guessing. On our dashboard, overall latency looked mildly worse, but breaking it down by endpoint showed p95 had roughly doubled on one: the order summary. That immediately told me it was not the load balancer or a general database problem.

Second, I looked at traces. I picked a slow request from after the release and a normal one from before and compared the spans. The extra time sat in one database call that appeared many times in the slow trace. That pointed at a query pattern, not a slow query.

Third, I read the release diff. A change to show per-item discounts had introduced a query inside a loop over order items: one query per item, an N+1 pattern. It had passed tests because our test orders contained one item and production orders average several.

Before fixing, I wanted proof, so I wrote a short script that created a ten-item order and measured the endpoint. It reproduced the slowdown. I replaced the loop with one batched query and added an index on the column we filtered by. I also considered a rollback, which would have been faster, but the release contained an unrelated fix we wanted to keep, so I told the team my plan and the risk, and shipped the forward fix with a review from a teammate.

After deployment p95 returned to its earlier level that afternoon, which I verified on the dashboard rather than assuming. Then I wrote a regression test that counts queries per request on that endpoint and fails above a limit, and I added multi-item orders to our test data.

What I changed afterwards: for any performance incident I now compare against the last known good version first, and hot endpoints have a query-count check. It has caught two similar mistakes since in review." *(Remove the last sentence unless it is true for you.)*

## Illustrative story B (fictional): choosing the simpler solution (AI flavour)

**Also fictional. Replace with your own story.**

**Five-bullet card**
1. **Context:** A small team building an internal assistant that answers HR policy questions. A planned design used a multi-step agent with tools.
2. **Responsibility:** I owned the design and the first implementation.
3. **Actions:** I wrote 40 real questions from the HR inbox and categorised them; most were lookups in a few policy documents. I built a baseline of retrieval plus one model call with citations in two days and evaluated it on the 40 questions. I showed the team the failure cases and which ones actually needed multi-step reasoning (a handful). I proposed shipping the simple pipeline first and adding an agent step only for those cases, with an eval to justify it.
4. **Result:** The simple pipeline answered most of the questions correctly with citations on my labelled set; the team shipped it in two weeks instead of the estimated six, and the agent idea was deferred with a clear trigger for revisiting. (Fictional; no real measurements.)
5. **Lesson:** Start with the simplest design that can pass a real eval, and let measured failures justify complexity.

**90-second version (about 200 words)**

"We were building an internal assistant for HR policy questions, and the initial design was a multi-step agent with several tools. I owned the design, and I was uneasy because nobody had looked at what employees actually asked. So I took forty real questions from the HR inbox and sorted them. Most were simple lookups in three or four documents.

I built a baseline in two days: retrieve the relevant passages, one model call, answers with citations. Then I evaluated it on those forty questions. It handled most of them correctly, and I wrote up the failures by category. A handful needed multi-step reasoning across documents.

I presented that to the team: here is what the simple version gets right, here are the cases where an agent would help, here is the cost and risk of the agent. We agreed to ship the simple pipeline first and only add an agent step for the failing category if the eval showed it paid off. We shipped in two weeks rather than the six we had estimated.

My lesson was to start with the simplest design that can pass a real evaluation, and let measured failures justify complexity."

**3-minute version (about 360 words)**

"The context was an internal assistant that answers HR policy questions: leave, expenses, benefits. A team of three engineers and one HR partner. The initial design on the whiteboard was a multi-step agent with several tools: a planner, a search tool, a calculator for leave balances, and a document fetcher. I owned the design and the first implementation.

I was uneasy for one reason: we had designed for questions we imagined, not the ones people asked. So before building anything, I asked HR for the last couple of months of questions from their inbox, took forty, and categorised them. The pattern was clear: most were lookups in three or four documents, a few needed information from two documents, and only a small number involved a calculation.

I then built the smallest thing that could be tested: retrieval over the policy documents, one model call with instructions to answer only from the passages and cite them. That took two days. I wrote the evaluation set from the forty questions with the document each answer should come from, and measured two things: did retrieval return the right document, and was the answer supported by it.

The simple version did well on the lookups. The failures fell into two groups: a few retrieval misses, which I fixed by adding keyword search to the vector search, and a few questions that really needed multi-step reasoning, such as combining a leave policy with a balance.

I took this to the team with a short document: what the simple version handles, where it fails, and what an agent would cost in complexity, latency and failure modes. Some colleagues preferred the agent. I did not argue against it in principle; I argued for sequence and evidence. We agreed to ship the simple pipeline, with a defined trigger: if the multi-step category exceeded a set share of real questions, we would add one agent step for it, and the eval would tell us if it helped.

We shipped in two weeks instead of the six we had estimated. The lesson I carry is to begin with the simplest design that can pass a real evaluation, and to treat added complexity as something measured failures must justify." *(Again, only keep claims that are true for you.)*

## Matrix: 6 to 8 stories covering 8 themes

Mark P for the primary story for a theme and B for a backup. The goal: every column has a P, most have a B, no story carries more than three themes.

| Story (placeholder titles) | Ownership | Debugging | Conflict | Failure | Prioritization | Learning | Communication | Quality |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Feature from ambiguity to launch | P | | | | B | | B | |
| 2. Production incident diagnosed | | P | | | | | | B |
| 3. Disagreement on design | | | P | | | | B | |
| 4. Rollback or missed estimate | | | | P | | B | | B |
| 5. Deadline versus tech debt | B | | | | P | | | |
| 6. New technology learned and used | | | | B | | P | | |
| 7. Risk explained to a non-technical stakeholder | | | B | | | | P | |
| 8. Test or monitoring change that prevented repeats | | B | | | | | | P |

If you only have six stories, merge: 1 and 5 (ownership plus prioritization), 7 into 3 (conflict plus communication), and 8 into 2 (debugging plus quality). Run `coverage` from `story_bank.py` to see which themes remain uncovered or single-story.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Worked example tab: a failure in the numbers or the code, a follow-up that changes a constraint, and the step you would skip under time. The stories were generic ('we had a tight deadline'). Action was a team we. Result had no number. Learning was 'communication is important'. Two stories contradicted the resume's dates. A conflict story blamed the other person. There were four stories, all from the same project, so a probe into a different company left them inventing.

## Interview follow-up

The interviewer just changed one number in the example. Interviewer: 'Tell me about a time you were wrong.' Outline: situation with a real constraint, the task you owned, the action you took (including the mistake), the result with a number or a clear outcome, and the learning you applied later. Follow-up: 'What would you do in the first week here?' Tie the learning to their environment, not a slogan.

## What you would cut

Ship the smallest version of this example that still teaches the mechanism. Cut borrowed stories and a sixth clone of the same incident. Keep six to eight true STAR-L cards that cover ownership, conflict, failure, and prioritisation, each with a result you can defend.

code.source:
import re

THEMES = ["ownership", "debugging", "conflict", "failure", "prioritization", "learning", "communication", "quality"]
FIELDS = ["context", "responsibility", "actions", "result", "lesson"]


def audit_story(s: dict) -> list:
    """s: {title, themes, context, responsibility, actions, result, lesson, metric_source}.
    Returns problems that would hurt you in an interview."""
    problems = []
    for f in FIELDS:
        if not s.get(f, "").strip():
            problems.append(f"missing {f}")
    text = " ".join(s.get(f, "") for f in FIELDS).lower()
    actions = s.get("actions", "").lower()
    we, i = len(re.findall(r"\bwe\b", actions)), len(re.findall(r"\bi\b", actions))
    if actions and we > i:
        problems.append("actions say 'we' more than 'I': make your own part explicit")
    if re.search(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])\d", s.get("result", "")) and not s.get("metric_source"):
        problems.append("result has a number but no metric_source: where was it measured?")
    if s.get("result") and not re.search(r"\d|reduc|increas|fewer|faster|shipped|adopted|stopped|prevented|learned", s["result"].lower()):
        problems.append("result is vague: say what changed and how you know")
    if re.search(r"\b(stupid|lazy|incompetent|idiot)\b", text):
        problems.append("blaming language: describe the situation, not the person")
    for t in s.get("themes", []):
        if t not in THEMES:
            problems.append(f"unknown theme {t}")
    return problems


def coverage(stories: list) -> dict:
    """Which themes have a story, which story is used for many themes, which themes are uncovered."""
    by_theme = {t: [s["title"] for s in stories if t in s.get("themes", [])] for t in THEMES}
    uncovered = [t for t, titles in by_theme.items() if not titles]
    thin = [t for t, titles in by_theme.items() if len(titles) == 1]   # only one story: no backup if asked twice
    return {"uncovered": uncovered, "single_story": thin, "by_theme": by_theme}


def check() -> None:
    good = {"title": "Checkout latency", "themes": ["debugging", "ownership"],
            "context": "Orders API p95 doubled after a release.",
            "responsibility": "I was on call and owned the service.",
            "actions": "I compared traces before and after, I found an N+1 query, I added an index and a regression test.",
            "result": "p95 returned to baseline within a day and the alert threshold was tightened.",
            "lesson": "Compare against a known good version first.", "metric_source": ""}
    assert audit_story(good) == []

    bad = dict(good, actions="We looked at it and we fixed it.", result="Latency fell 50%", metric_source="")
    problems = audit_story(bad)
    assert any("'we'" in p for p in problems)
    assert any("metric_source" in p for p in problems)

    stories = [good, dict(good, title="Pushed back on agent", themes=["communication", "prioritization"]),
               dict(good, title="Rollback fail", themes=["failure", "learning", "quality"])]
    cov = coverage(stories)
    assert cov["uncovered"] == ["conflict"]
    assert "debugging" in cov["single_story"]
    print("story bank: all checks passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    check()

parts.body:
## How to use this section

Pick a story from your bank, say it aloud with a timer, then have someone ask the follow-ups below. Behavioural answers are graded on specifics, so rehearse with your own facts. The model answers here are structured guides, not scripts to copy, and any example is fictional.

For each prompt, the structure is: **Define** (what the question is really testing), **Mechanism** (how to answer), **Decision** (which story), **Trade-off**, **Evidence**, then the spoken version and follow-ups.

## Prompt 1. A time an LLM feature misbehaved

**Define.** Tests whether you treat LLM output as untrusted, debug non-deterministic systems systematically, and build prevention.

**Mechanism.** Describe the feature and the misbehaviour precisely (wrong answer, ungrounded citation, refusal, format break, cost spike). Then your investigation: reproduce with logged inputs, check which stage failed (retrieval, prompt, model, parser), form a hypothesis, test it on a small eval set. Then the fix and the prevention: a test case added to the eval set, a validator, a guardrail or a monitoring signal.

**Decision.** Use a debugging plus quality story. If you have no production LLM story, use a project or prototype and say so; do not pretend.

**Trade-off.** Fixing the prompt is fast but fragile; fixing retrieval or adding validation is slower but more durable. Say which you chose and why.

**Evidence.** The eval set entry, the trace or log, the PR. Mention what you measured before and after only if you did.

**60-90 second version (structure):** "[Feature] sometimes [symptom]. I reproduced it by [logged inputs], found it was [stage], tested [hypothesis] on [N] cases. I fixed it by [action], added the failing cases to the eval set and a [validator or alert]. The result: [measured change or honest qualitative outcome]. I now treat every model output as untrusted input and add a regression case for each failure."

**Follow-ups.** *How did you know it was fixed?* Describe the eval and its limits. *Could it recur?* What guard prevents it. *What did you not understand?* Be honest about residual uncertainty.

## Prompt 2. A time you pushed back on hype

**Define.** Tests judgement under pressure, ability to disagree constructively, and communication of risk to non-experts.

**Mechanism.** State the pressure ("use an agent for everything", "ship before the demo", "claim 95% accuracy"). Describe how you converted opinion into evidence: a small experiment, a labelled set, a cost estimate or a failure demo. Show that you understood the other side's goal and offered an alternative path, not just a no. Say what was decided and whether you committed even if you lost.

**Decision.** Choose a story where you were respectful and data-driven. **Trade-off:** pushing back costs social capital; unprompted agreement costs the product. **Evidence:** the document, the experiment, the outcome. If the outcome was mixed, say so.

**60-90 second version (structure):** "The goal was [X]; the suggestion was [hyped approach]. I was concerned about [risk]. Instead of arguing, I [ran a small test / estimated cost / showed failure cases]. That showed [finding]. I proposed [alternative with a path to the ambitious goal]. We [outcome]. What I learned is to bring evidence and an alternative."

**Follow-ups.** *What if they had overruled you?* I would state my concern in writing, agree on a measurable checkpoint, and commit. *Were you wrong at any point?* Share an honest correction if you have one.

## Prompt 3. A time you chose the simpler solution

**Define.** Tests engineering maturity: matching complexity to need. **Mechanism:** the story of illustrative story B in the Worked example is the model: gather real inputs, build a baseline, evaluate, let failures justify complexity. **Decision:** prioritisation plus ownership. **Trade-off:** simpler ships faster but may cap quality; define the trigger to revisit. **Evidence:** the baseline's eval result and the shipped timeline.

**60-90 second version (structure):** "We were planning [complex]. I asked what real cases looked like, built [simple baseline] in [time], evaluated on [N] real cases, and showed [what worked, what didn't]. We shipped the simple version and defined [trigger] for adding complexity."

**Follow-ups.** *What did you give up?* Name the cases not handled. *How did you convince others?* Evidence, not opinion.

## Follow-up question bank, with answers

| Follow-up | How to answer |
|---|---|
| What was your exact role? | Name your title for this work, what you owned, and what others owned. "I owned X; Priya owned Y." |
| What would you do differently? | One specific change plus why, ideally something you later did. Avoid "nothing" and avoid trivia |
| Who disagreed, and why were they right or wrong? | Describe their goal fairly; say what they were right about |
| How did you know it worked? | A metric, dashboard, test or user feedback, with its limits. If unmeasured: "I did not measure it formally; the signal was..." |
| What was the hardest part? | The decision under uncertainty, not the typing |
| What was the impact on the business or users? | Concrete effect, scaled honestly; say "small team tool" if that is what it was |
| What did you not know at the time? | Show humility and learning |
| How long did it take, and what was the deadline? | Real timeline; it shows you know trade-offs |
| Did anyone help you? | Credit others by name; shows maturity, not weakness |
| What would have happened if you had done nothing? | The risk you avoided; do not exaggerate |
| Can I talk to someone who worked with you on that? | Say yes only if you mean it |
| Tell me about a time you were wrong. | Choose a real, bounded mistake, own it, show the change |
| How would this scale or repeat on a bigger team? | Process change you would make: owner, review, monitoring |
| Why did you choose that over alternatives? | Two options, your criteria, the trade-off accepted |
| What did you learn that you still use? | A habit with an example from a later project |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Why it hurts | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **We versus I** | The interviewer cannot tell what you did | Say "we" for the goal and "I" for your steps; name your boundary |
| **No result** | The story ends at the action, so there is no evidence of impact | State what changed and how you know, even if modest |
| **Blame** | Signals you will blame them next | Describe constraints and incentives; own your part |
| **Invented or inflated metrics** | Collapses under a follow-up and ends trust | Source every number; use qualitative evidence when no number exists |
| **Memorised monologue** | Sounds robotic, cannot adapt to the question | Memorise the five bullets, not sentences |
| **Backstory overload** | No time left for actions | Two sentences of context |
| **Generic lesson** | "Communication is key" tells them nothing | One concrete changed behaviour |
| **Hero story with no team** | Looks like poor collaboration | Credit others and show how you worked with them |
| **Choosing a trivial story** | No decision to examine | Pick one with a trade-off |
| **Always the same story** | Reveals a thin bank | Use the matrix and the backups |

## Rehearsal protocol

1. Day 1: write five-bullet cards for all stories, run `story_bank.py`, fix the flags.
2. Day 2: 90-second versions out loud, recorded; count "we" and filler.
3. Day 3: 3-minute versions for the four most likely themes; ask a friend to interrupt with the bank's follow-ups.
4. Weekly: one random theme, cold, two minutes.
5. Before each interview: re-read the cards for the role's likely themes; for an AI role add the three AI-flavoured prompts.

## Worked failure

Use this on the Interview tab: a spoken-answer failure, the actual next question, and the essay you would not say out loud. The stories were generic ('we had a tight deadline'). Action was a team we. Result had no number. Learning was 'communication is important'. Two stories contradicted the resume's dates. A conflict story blamed the other person. There were four stories, all from the same project, so a probe into a different company left them inventing.

## Interview follow-up

You already gave a 90-second answer; this is the probe. Interviewer: 'Tell me about a time you were wrong.' Outline: situation with a real constraint, the task you owned, the action you took (including the mistake), the result with a number or a clear outcome, and the learning you applied later. Follow-up: 'What would you do in the first week here?' Tie the learning to their environment, not a slogan.

## What you would cut

Say less: keep define, mechanism, decision, trade-off, evidence. Cut borrowed stories and a sixth clone of the same incident. Keep six to eight true STAR-L cards that cover ownership, conflict, failure, and prioritisation, each with a result you can defend.

# Drills

Two cards, spoken, 90 seconds each. Name Situation, Task, Action, Result, Learning out loud so you notice if one is missing.

## Prompt 1 — closed-book

"Tell me about a time a GenAI feature failed in front of a user or a reviewer."

**Model outline:**
- **S.** A real setting (internal demo, ticket, on-call), with a constraint (time, customer, data).
- **T.** The outcome you owned (quality, a rollback, a communication).
- **A.** What you did: looked at traces or retrieved chunks, wrote a failing case, changed a gate or a prompt, told someone.
- **R.** A result that can be checked (eval moved, incident closed, feature flagged off). If you have no number, say the concrete outcome.
- **L.** A rule you still use (no release without a replayable case; never trust tool args).
- **Would not.** Blame "the model" with no artefact, or a story that contradicts your resume.

## Prompt 2 — closed-book

"Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate on RAG versus fine-tuning (or another design choice) and what you did."

**Model outline:**
- **S.** Two options on the table, a deadline, a user.
- **T.** Decide or run a test, not win the argument.
- **A.** You proposed a cheap comparison (prompt/RAG baseline vs a small fine-tune), defined the metric, and time-boxed it.
- **R.** The option you shipped and the metric that justified it; include if you lost the argument and still supported the ship.
- **L.** Disagreements die with a test, not a slide.
- **Check.** Names and dates match the resume. If you have not had this fight, use a true smaller disagreement (chunk size, top_k) and say so.

After both, mark any story that lacks a result or a learning as unusable until you fix it.

lessons.title: Readiness Gates and Weekly Scoring
lessons.summary: Use evidence-based readiness gates per domain and a 0-5 weekly score, a Sunday review ritual and clear decision rules to prepare honestly.
keyPoints: Replace 'I studied X' with testable gates per domain: Python/SQL, LLM fundamentals, RAG, agents, production, system design, project defense and behavioral.
Score 0 not studied, 1 recognise, 2 explain with notes, 3 explain closed-book, 4 implement or debug, 5 handle follow-ups and trade-offs.
Target 3 or more across core domains and 4 or more in your strongest project; this is a useful target, not a guarantee of an offer.
If a domain is below 3, schedule two focused sessions the following week; do not compensate with more unrelated tutorials.
Score from evidence after a closed-book attempt, take the lower score when torn, and freeze the definitions so the trend stays meaningful.
Look at the minimum domain and the trend: a drop means decay, three flat weeks below target means change the method.
Anti-patterns are tutorial hoarding and framework collecting; the antidote is one measurable artifact per week.
In interviews, describe self-assessment honestly: what you measured, what you only believe and what you changed.

check.q: At your Sunday review you score RAG at 2 and agents at 1, and every other domain is at 3 or above. What does the rule say to do next week?
options: Spend the week on the strongest domain to build confidence
Watch new courses on both topics to cover the gaps
Lower the scoring standard so the scores reach 3
Schedule two focused sessions in each domain below 3 and skip unrelated tutorials
check.why: The rule is two focused sessions the following week for any domain below 3, without compensating by consuming unrelated material. Strengthening a strong domain or moving the goalposts hides the gap.

check.q: What separates a score of 3 from a score of 4 in a domain such as RAG?
options: A 3 is explaining closed-book; a 4 is having implemented or debugged it
A 3 requires a certificate; a 4 requires a job
A 3 is explaining with notes; a 4 is explaining closed-book
There is no difference; the numbers are only motivational
check.why: Score 3 means you can explain it from memory. Score 4 means you have built or diagnosed a real bug without a tutorial. Explaining with notes is a 2.

check.q: Your system design score has been 2 for three weeks despite reading many write-ups. What is the best decision?
options: Read more write-ups until the score rises
Change the method: do timed designs aloud, record them and compare to a checklist
Stop scoring that domain
Redefine the score of 2 as a 3
check.why: A flat score after more reading shows the method is the problem. Production practice (timed, aloud, recorded, checked) moves explanation and trade-off skills. Redefining scores destroys the trend.

parts.body:
> **Outcome:** Use evidence-based readiness gates per domain and a 0-5 weekly score, a Sunday review ritual and clear decision rules to prepare honestly.
> **Prerequisites:** None; use from week 1.
> **Estimated time:** 35 min reading, then the hands-on task. Apply it once in your next weekly review or mock, using the lesson's worked example or template.

## Why readiness gates exist

Preparation fails in a predictable way: you feel busy and productive because you watched or read a lot, while the skills an interviewer tests (explaining closed-book, implementing, debugging, defending trade-offs) did not move. **Readiness gates** replace "I studied X" with "I can demonstrate Y". A gate is a statement you can test on yourself in one sitting. A **weekly readiness score** turns the gates into a number per domain so you can see trends and make decisions instead of guessing.

The targets below are useful targets, not guarantees. Interviews have noise, other candidates and luck. The gates make your effort measurable; they do not promise an offer.

## The gates: you are ready when

| Domain | You are ready when you can |
|---|---|
| Python and SQL | Solve common problems independently, explain time and space complexity, and write tests. SQL answers are correct under time limits. |
| LLM fundamentals | Explain tokenization, attention, embeddings, inference, hallucinations and model adaptation clearly, closed-book. |
| RAG | Build the pipeline, diagnose retrieval versus generation failure, measure quality, and explain how permissions are enforced. |
| Agents | Implement bounded tool use, explain state and stop conditions, trace failures, and enforce human approval where needed. |
| Production | Containerize and deploy, and discuss secrets, retries, logging, monitoring, latency, cost and provider failure. |
| System design | Clarify requirements, draw the architecture, estimate key costs, identify bottlenecks and defend trade-offs. |
| Project defense | Demonstrate the project and answer detailed questions about every major design choice, honestly. |
| Behavioral | Tell 6-8 real stories with clear personal actions, results and lessons. |

## The 0-5 score

| Score | Meaning | Test |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Not studied | You could not start an answer |
| 1 | Recognise terms | You know the words when you see them |
| 2 | Explain with notes | You can explain it with the material open |
| 3 | Explain closed-book | You explain it from memory, in order, in two minutes |
| 4 | Implement or debug | You built it, or diagnosed a real bug in it, without a tutorial |
| 5 | Handle follow-ups and trade-offs | You survive a hostile interviewer's "why not X?" and "what breaks at 10x?" |

**Targets.** Aim for **3 or more across the core domains** and **4 or more in your strongest project** (the Project defense domain). **Rule:** if a domain is below 3, schedule **two focused sessions the following week** in that domain. Do not compensate with more unrelated tutorials.

Score honestly. A score is "what I demonstrated this week", not "what I once knew" and not "what I could probably recall".

## Evidence checklist per domain and level

For each cell, the evidence is something you can show or do, not a feeling. Levels 0 and 1 are deliberately thin: there is little to show.

### Python and SQL

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | Nothing attempted this week |
| 1 | You recognise the pattern name (two pointers, window function) when you see a solution |
| 2 | You solve with a hint or notes; you can explain a solution you read |
| 3 | Closed-book, you solve a medium problem unaided in the time limit and state its complexity; a CTE or window query is written correctly |
| 4 | You have tests (including edge cases) for your solution and a timed SQL set with a pass log; you fixed a bug found by a test |
| 5 | You answer follow-ups: alternative approach, worst-case input, index choice and `EXPLAIN` reading |

### LLM fundamentals

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | Nothing this week |
| 1 | You recognise token, attention, embedding, temperature |
| 2 | You explain each with the notes open |
| 3 | A two-minute closed-book explanation of each, including one number (for example context-window arithmetic) |
| 4 | You implemented a tokenizer count or a tiny attention computation, or measured token cost on real prompts |
| 5 | You handle "why do hallucinations happen", "fine-tune vs RAG vs prompt" trade-offs with evidence |

### RAG

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | Nothing this week |
| 1 | You recognise chunk, retriever, rerank, citation |
| 2 | You describe the pipeline from notes |
| 3 | You draw the pipeline from memory and explain permission filtering and abstention |
| 4 | A working prototype with tests, a labelled eval set and a failure report with before/after |
| 5 | You defend chunking, hybrid, rerank and threshold choices with your measurements and survive follow-ups |

### Agents

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | Nothing this week |
| 1 | You recognise tool call, loop, planner |
| 2 | You explain the loop with notes |
| 3 | You explain state, stop conditions and approval gates closed-book |
| 4 | An agent with bounded steps, validated tool inputs, a trace, and a debugged failure you can narrate |
| 5 | You discuss failure containment, cost bounds, evaluation of trajectories and when not to use an agent |

### Production

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | Nothing this week |
| 1 | You recognise container, retry, timeout, metric |
| 2 | You explain a deployment with notes |
| 3 | You list closed-book how secrets, retries with backoff, logs, metrics, latency and provider failure are handled |
| 4 | A container you built and deployed, with a health check, structured logs and one failure you injected and handled |
| 5 | You answer capacity, cost-per-request and incident follow-ups with numbers labelled as estimates or measurements |

### System design

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | Nothing this week |
| 1 | You recognise the building blocks |
| 2 | You follow a worked design with notes |
| 3 | In 40 minutes you clarify requirements, draw a design and name bottlenecks, unaided |
| 4 | You also did a back-of-envelope estimate (requests, tokens, cost, storage) and revised the design because of it |
| 5 | You defend each choice against alternatives and say what you would measure first |

### Project defense

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | No project to discuss |
| 1 | You can describe what it does |
| 2 | You explain the architecture with the code open |
| 3 | You explain every major choice and its alternative from memory |
| 4 | You demo it live, show tests and metrics, and say honestly what is unfinished or unmeasured |
| 5 | A hostile reviewer asks "why not X" for ten minutes and you answer with evidence or an honest "I did not test that; here is how I would" |

### Behavioral

| Level | What you can show |
|---|---|
| 0 | No stories written |
| 1 | You have a list of events |
| 2 | Stories written with notes (situation, task, action, result, lesson) |
| 3 | 6-8 real stories told from memory in about two minutes, each with your personal actions |
| 4 | Stories recorded or told to another person, tightened after feedback, each with a verifiable result and a lesson |
| 5 | You adapt a story to the question asked, handle probing about your role versus the team's, and never invent a metric |

## Failure modes of self-scoring

| Mistake | Effect | Counter |
|---|---|---|
| Scoring what you recognise as what you can produce | Inflated 3s | Score only after a closed-book attempt |
| Scoring once a month | Late warning | Every Sunday, same ritual |
| Scoring against the best day | Optimism | Use the weakest evidence from this week |
| Only improving favourite domains | A hidden 1 sinks the loop | Look at the minimum, not the average |
| Changing the rubric when scores are low | Meaningless trend | Freeze the definitions |

## Worked failure

Use this on the Concepts tab: a failure born from misunderstanding the idea, a follow-up that probes the definition, and the extra theory you would drop. Sunday scoring was done from memory: everything a 4 because the week 'felt productive'. The gate for RAG (explain closed-book plus an eval artifact) was marked done after reading. Next week's plan ignored the 2 on agents. The score sheet was not saved. A month later they could not show a trend. They scheduled applications while three core gates were still at 1.

## Interview follow-up

Ask this after you close the tab. Interviewer (self): 'Which gate is actually below 3, and what is Tuesday's drill?' Outline: name the domain, the evidence that is missing (spoken answer, artifact, mock dimension), and the first task. Follow-up: 'Why are you applying this week?' Answer only if the must-have gates for that role family are at 3 or you are explicit that you are practising screens.

## What you would cut

If this part is running long, drop background that does not change a decision. Cut a new topic that is not on a weak gate. Keep the eight domains, a saved 0-5 sheet, and next week's drills tied to scores of 2 or below.
